134.title: If people knew
134.hook: if beings knew the fruit of giving, they would not eat without sharing (Itivuttaka 26)
134.howItsDone: Some Buddhists set aside part of a meal to offer first, at a home shrine, to monks or to guests, and sharing food is an everyday form of dana.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sumana, glad three times: glad before giving, bright while giving, uplifted after. Your line was glad before, bright during, happy after. Did you catch all three moments once? Day one hundred thirty-four.
screen: `SUMANA — GLAD BEFORE, BRIGHT DURING, HAPPY AFTER.`

segments.voice: One slice of pizza left in the box. Four people around the table. Everybody saw it. Nobody's reaching. A tiny standoff, polite and a little ridiculous. Someone finally says, go on, split it? Now the same slice at midnight, alone in the kitchen: it's simply gone, no thought at all. The Buddha said something about that last bite, a line so strong that it can sound almost impossible. It's in a small book of his sayings, and it opens with a condition: if people knew.
screen: `THE LAST SLICE IN THE BOX.` → `A TINY STANDOFF.` → `IF PEOPLE KNEW.`

segments.voice: The book is the Itivuttaka, which means this was said, a collection of short teachings the tradition remembers as the Buddha's own words. In saying twenty-six, he says, in substance: if beings knew, as I know, the result of giving and sharing, they would not eat without first giving. The stain of stinginess would not take hold of their minds. Even if it were their last bite, their last mouthful, they would not eat it without sharing, if there were someone to share it with. But because they don't know, he says, they eat without giving, and stinginess stains their minds. Notice what this teaching is, and what it isn't. It isn't a rule: you must share. It's a claim about knowledge. The problem isn't that people are bad. It's that they don't see what giving actually does. If they could see it, sharing would be as obvious as stepping out of the rain. What does giving do? The texts talk about good results in this life and future lives. But they also point to something anyone can check tonight. The saying calls stinginess a stain, and it can sit in the body as something tight and small. Sharing loosens it. Back to the last slice. When someone finally splits it, the whole table relaxes. Nobody got much pizza. Everybody got something better. And look at the word the saying uses: the last bite. Not the leftovers, not what you didn't want. Sharing the last of something is where generosity stops being easy and starts being real.
screen: `ITIVUTTAKA: THIS WAS SAID.` · `IF THEY KNEW THE FRUIT OF GIVING.` · `NOT A COMMAND, A WAY OF SEEING.` · `STINGINESS IS A STAIN.` · then, large: `SHARE THE LAST BITE.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Think of something you usually keep to yourself: the last cookie, the good seat, the end of the coffee, an hour of quiet. Notice whether a little tightness comes when you imagine giving it away. Don't fight it; just feel where it sits in the body. Then picture yourself sharing it anyway, and the other person's surprise. Notice what happens to the tightness. Breathe with whatever you find. The bell holds the time.
Samvibhaga. Sharing, dividing out: the Buddha's saying that if beings knew the fruit of giving, they wouldn't eat even their last bite without it.
Your line: share the last bite. Today, share part of a meal: half a sandwich, the last slice, a coffee for the person next to you. Day one hundred thirty-four.

what it means: a claim about seeing clearly; if we knew what giving does, we couldn't help sharing.
what a scholar hears: Itivuttaka 26 pairs dana with samvibhaga, sharing, and calls stinginess (macchera) a stain (mala) on the mind.

135.title: Giving attention
135.hook: the most common gift is simply listening
135.howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers describe attentive listening as a form of generosity, and the texts praise giving 'respectfully', with care, as part of what makes any gift a good one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, samvibhaga, if people knew: if beings saw the fruit of giving, they'd share even the last bite. Your line was share the last bite. Did someone get half your sandwich? Day one hundred thirty-five.

When did someone last really listen to you? Not nodding while typing. Not waiting for their turn. Really listening: their phone somewhere else, their eyes on you, a question that showed they'd heard. For some people the answer is a name and a day, weeks back. This week is about dana, giving, and so far it's been food and things. But there's a gift almost nobody thinks of as a gift, and it costs nothing except the one thing we're shortest on. Today: attention.
screen: `WHO REALLY LISTENED TO YOU?` → `A NAME, WEEKS BACK.` → `A GIFT THAT COSTS NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Let's be honest about the sources first. The old lists of gifts in the Pali texts talk about food, drink, clothing, shelter, lamps, medicine, and above all the gift of the teaching. They don't have a sermon titled listening is giving. But they come very close. In one discourse, the Buddha describes the gift of a good person, and the first thing on the list isn't what you give but how. A good person gives with faith, gives respectfully, gives at the right time, gives with a generous heart, and gives without harming anyone. That word, respectfully, sakkacca in Pali, means with care, with attention, with your whole self in it. A bowl of rice tossed carelessly and a bowl of rice offered with care are not the same gift. The attention is part of what's given. Another list names four ways that hold a community together: giving, kind speech, helpful action, and treating people as equals. Three of the four are about how you are with people, not what you hand them. Put those together and you arrive where some Buddhist teachers today arrive: attention is a gift. Anyone can give it. Nobody can give it while doing something else. And it has a strange property. When you give someone your full attention, you also get to be fully somewhere yourself. It's the practice you've been doing on the cushion, the breath, the feet, turned toward a person: the same steady noticing, pointed at someone's face instead of your own breath.
screen: `THE OLD LISTS: FOOD, LAMPS, TEACHING.` · `SAKKACCA: GIVING WITH CARE.` · `FOUR THINGS THAT HOLD PEOPLE TOGETHER.` · `THE CUSHION, TURNED TOWARD A PERSON.` · then, large: `ATTENTION IS A GIFT.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. For the first part of this sit, give your full attention to the sounds around you, one at a time, the way you'd listen to a friend. Don't name them or judge them. Just receive them. Then bring to mind one person you'll see today. Picture sitting with them, phone away, eyes on them, listening all the way to the end of their sentence before you answer. Notice how it feels even to imagine it. The bell holds the time.
Giving attention. The gift of full presence: listening with care, the way the texts say a good person gives, respectfully.
Your line: attention is a gift. Today, give one person your full attention for one whole conversation: the phone face down, listening to the end of every sentence. Day one hundred thirty-five.

136.title: The poor woman's lamp
136.hook: a Mahayana story: a beggar's cheap lamp burns all night after the king's lamps go out
136.howItsDone: The story of the poor woman's lamp is told widely in East Asian and Tibetan Buddhism, and many temples invite visitors to offer a single lamp or candle, however small the donation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, giving attention: the gift almost nobody counts, given with care. Your line was attention is a gift. Did one person get your whole attention, phone face down? Day one hundred thirty-six.

Have you ever stood in a line to give something, and felt small? The fundraiser where everyone else writes a big check. The birthday where your present is the homemade one. The wedding registry where the good things are already gone. There's a quiet shame in giving little when others give a lot. Today's story is about exactly that feeling. It's not from the Pali texts we've mostly been reading. It comes down through the northern traditions, and it's told in China, Japan, Korea and Tibet.
screen: `EVERYONE ELSE WRITES A BIG CHECK.` → `YOURS IS THE HOMEMADE ONE.` → `A STORY FROM THE NORTH AND EAST.`

segments.voice: Here's the story, as it's told in a Chinese collection called the Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish. The Buddha is staying near a city, and the king wants to honor him with light. He orders oil lamps lit, row after row, along the road and around the monastery. A poor woman, often called Nanda, sees the preparations and longs to give something too. But she has nothing. She begs all day and gets one small coin. She takes it to the oil seller, who tells her it's not enough for anything worth having. When she explains what it's for, he's moved and gives her more than the coin could buy. It's still just enough for one small lamp. She sets it among the king's lamps and makes a wish with her whole heart: that her lamp, like the Buddha's teaching, might bring light to others. Through the night, the king's lamps burn out, one by one. By dawn, only hers is still burning. The Buddha's disciple Maudgalyayana, famous for his powers, comes at daybreak to put the lamps out. He tries with his hand, with his robe, with a fan. It won't go out. The Buddha tells him to stop: that lamp was lit with a great heart, and no wind could put it out. The point isn't that small gifts are better than large ones. The king's lamps were real gifts. The point is that the measure of a gift isn't its size. It's how much of yourself is in it. In Japan there's still an old saying: better the poor one's single lamp than the rich one's ten thousand.
screen: `THE KING'S ROWS OF LAMPS.` · `ONE COIN, ONE SMALL LAMP.` · `AT DAWN, ONLY HERS BURNS.` · `NOT THE SIZE, BUT THE HEART.` · then, large: `SMALL AND WHOLEHEARTED.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Picture a small oil lamp in front of you: a clay dish, a wick, a single flame. Watch it steady itself with each breath. Now bring to mind something small you could give today, something that feels almost too little to count. A note. A phone call. A single flower. Hold it the way the poor woman held her coin. Put your whole heart into the intention. Let the flame and the breath burn together. The bell holds the time.
The poor woman's lamp. A beggar's single lamp, lit with her whole heart, that burned all night after the king's lamps went out.
Your line: small and wholehearted. Today, give one small thing with your whole heart in it, and don't apologize for its size. Day one hundred thirty-six.

the king orders it put out.

137.title: Giving without a receipt
137.hook: give, and let it go; don't keep score
137.howItsDone: Some Buddhists give anonymously or without expecting return, and in Mahayana traditions the perfection of giving is described as giving without clinging to the gift, the receiver or the self as giver.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the poor woman's lamp: one small flame, lit with a whole heart, still burning at dawn. Your line was small and wholehearted. What small thing did you give? Day one hundred thirty-seven, the end of the giving week.
screen: `THE POOR WOMAN'S LAMP — SMALL AND WHOLEHEARTED.`

segments.voice: There's a ledger that's easy to keep and hard to admit to. I drove last time. I paid for dinner twice. I remembered her birthday; she forgot mine. It's not greed exactly. It's bookkeeping. And the ledger has a way of turning gifts into loans. You gave, but somewhere in the back office, it was written down, with a due date. This whole week has been about giving. It ends with the hardest part, the part that decides whether a gift stays a gift: what happens after you let go.
screen: `I DROVE LAST TIME.` → `THE LEDGER IN THE BACK OFFICE.` → `WHAT HAPPENS AFTER YOU LET GO.`

segments.voice: In one discourse, Sariputta asks the Buddha why the same gift can bear great fruit for one person and little for another. The Buddha answers with a ladder of motives. Someone gives hoping to get something back, or thinking I'll enjoy the reward of this later. That's a gift, and it bears some fruit. Higher up, someone gives simply because giving is good, or because it's the family custom, or to follow the example of wise people of old, or because it makes the mind clear and glad. And at the top, someone gives as an ornament and a support for the mind. Same rice, same bowl. What changes is what the giver is holding onto. A later Mahayana text, the Diamond Sutra, pushes it further. It says a bodhisattva should give without dwelling on anything: not on sights, not on sounds, not on anything the mind could grab. Later teachers put it as three things held lightly: the giver, the gift, the receiver. Give like a hand that opens and doesn't close again to check what it gave. Teachers sometimes call it giving that leaves no trace. The Pali word for that kind of generosity is caga, which also means letting go, relinquishing. Generosity and letting go are the same word. So look back at the week. Giving first opens the door. The bowl is open. Glad three times, glad before, bright during, happy after. Share the last bite. Attention is a gift. Small and wholehearted. And now, the last step: no receipt. Nobody's saying you can't notice who never pays. You can still be wise. But the gift itself, once it leaves your hand, is finished. It doesn't need a signature.
screen: `A LADDER OF MOTIVES.` · `AT THE TOP: AN ORNAMENT FOR THE MIND.` · `GIVE WITHOUT DWELLING ON ANYTHING.` · `CAGA: GENEROSITY IS LETTING GO.` · then, large: `NO RECEIPT.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one gift you're still keeping track of: a favor that wasn't returned, a kindness nobody noticed. See it written as a line in the ledger, with a date beside it. Now, with the out-breath, imagine tearing up the receipt. Not because they deserved it, but because the gift was already complete. Breathe out again, and let the hand open. Rest in whatever lightness comes. The bell holds the time.
Caga. Generosity, letting go: giving without a receipt, no score kept, the gift complete the moment it leaves your hand.
Your line: no receipt. Today, give one thing anonymously: pay for a stranger's coffee, leave a note unsigned, fix something nobody will know you fixed. Day one hundred thirty-seven.

it bears some fruit; the fruit grows as the motive becomes freer.

generosity and relinquishing are the same word.

fork.reveal: he describes a ladder of motives, from hoping for a return up to giving as an ornament for the mind.

what it means: give and let go; the gift is complete when it leaves your hand.

138.title: Homage
138.hook: homage to the Blessed One, the worthy one, the fully awakened: the opening chant
138.howItsDone: In Theravada temples and homes, the line 'Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa' is chanted three times at the start of almost every ceremony, before the refuges and precepts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, caga, giving without a receipt, the end of the giving week. Your line was no receipt. Did you give one thing nobody will ever trace to you? Day one hundred thirty-eight, and a new week: the chant and the shrine.

Walk into a Theravada temple almost anywhere, in Colombo, Bangkok, Yangon, or a converted house in Ohio, and the first sound you'll likely hear is the same line of Pali, chanted slowly, three times. Before the refuges. Before the precepts. Before a talk, a blessing, a meal. It's the doorbell of Buddhist practice, the words people use to walk in. Many people who've heard it a hundred times couldn't tell you what it means. Today we open it, word by word.
screen: `COLOMBO, BANGKOK, OHIO.` → `THE SAME LINE, THREE TIMES.` → `THE DOORBELL OF PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Here it is: Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa. Five words. Namo: homage, a bow in a word. It's the same root you hear in namaste. Tassa: to him, to that one. Bhagavato: the Blessed One, the fortunate one, the title people used for the Buddha while he lived. Arahato: the worthy one, the arahant, the one who has put down greed, hatred and delusion. And sammasambuddhassa: the one fully and rightly awakened, by himself. Put together: homage to the Blessed One, the worthy one, the fully awakened one. Three titles, each saying a little more. It's chanted three times, and many people say each round as a small bow of the mind. The line is ancient. In the Middle Discourses, a Brahmin woman named Dhananjani is so devoted to the Buddha that when she stumbles, the words that come out of her mouth are this line, three times, the way someone else might say oh my goodness. A young Brahmin named Sangarava hears her and is not impressed, and the story that follows is his meeting with the Buddha. So the chant isn't a password. It's what devotion sounds like when it overflows. Why begin with homage? Because it sets the direction before anything else happens. Before you ask for anything or learn anything, you turn toward what you value. Buddhists say homage to the Buddha is not worship of a god; it's respect for a human being who woke up, and for the possibility that anyone can.
screen: `NAMO: HOMAGE, A BOW IN A WORD.` · `BLESSED, WORTHY, FULLY AWAKE.` · `DHANANJANI STUMBLES AND SAYS IT.` · `TURN TOWARD WHAT YOU VALUE.` · then, large: `HOMAGE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. If you'd like, chant the line three times, slowly, the way it's chanted in temples: Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa. If you'd rather not chant, just listen as it's said, and let each of the three titles land: blessed, worthy, awake. Then rest in the silence afterward. Notice the mind turned in one direction, like a plant toward light. The bell holds the time.
Namo tassa. The opening homage: to the Blessed One, the worthy one, the fully awakened one, chanted three times.
Your line: a bow in a word. Today, before one thing you begin, a meal, a sitting, a hard task, pause and turn toward what you value most, even for one breath. Day one hundred thirty-eight.

139.title: The home shrine
139.hook: an image, a candle, incense, a flower, water: a small corner
139.howItsDone: Many Buddhist households keep a small shrine with a Buddha image placed high and clean, and offer a candle, incense, flowers and water there each day; Japanese families often keep a butsudan cabinet that also honors ancestors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, namo tassa, the opening homage: to the Blessed One, the worthy one, the fully awakened. Your line was a bow in a word. Did you pause before beginning something and turn toward what you value? Day one hundred thirty-nine.
screen: `NAMO TASSA — A BOW IN A WORD.`

segments.voice: Every home already has shrines. We just don't call them that. The fridge door with the kids' drawings and the save-the-date. The shelf with a grandparent's photo and a candle that's never lit. The nightstand where the phone sleeps, glowing, the first thing you touch every morning. We arrange our small altars without thinking, and then they arrange us. Buddhist homes, from Sri Lanka to Japan to a studio apartment in Denver, often keep one corner arranged on purpose. Today: the home shrine.
screen: `THE FRIDGE DOOR. THE NIGHTSTAND.` → `WE ALREADY HAVE ALTARS.` → `ONE CORNER, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: A home shrine can be tiny. A shelf, the top of a bookcase, a corner of a table. The traditional pieces are simple. An image of the Buddha, often seated in meditation. A candle or small lamp. Incense. A flower. Clean water in a small bowl or cup. We'll open the flower, the candle and the incense later this week, so today is about the space itself. A few customs come up again and again. The image goes somewhere high and clean, often at or above head height when you're seated, never on the floor, never in a bathroom or next to shoes. It's kept dusted. Fresh flowers replace wilted ones. Some people put the shrine where they'll see it first in the morning. Traditions differ in the details. In Tibetan homes you may see a row of seven small bowls of water, filled each morning and emptied in the evening. In Japan, families may keep a butsudan, a wooden cabinet that holds a Buddha image along with the names of family members who have died. In Theravada homes, the shrine may hold a small Buddha image, a photo of a respected teacher, and the day's offerings. What's the image for? Buddhist teachers say it isn't a god and it isn't magic. It's a reminder: of the Buddha, of what's possible, of the practice you meant to do today. The shrine turns a corner of the house into a place where the mind remembers what it's for. It doesn't need to be expensive or beautiful. It needs to be clean, and cared for, and yours.
screen: `AN IMAGE, A CANDLE, INCENSE, A FLOWER, WATER.` · `HIGH, CLEAN, NEVER ON THE FLOOR.` · `SEVEN BOWLS; A CABINET; A SHELF.` · `NOT A GOD: A REMINDER.` · then, large: `A QUIET CORNER.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Now, in your mind, walk through your home and look for a small space that could be a quiet corner. A shelf, a windowsill, the top of a dresser. Somewhere clean and a little above your head when you sit. Picture it cleared. Picture what you might put there: an image, a stone, a candle, a cup of water, whatever means something to you. Rest with the breath in that imagined corner. The bell holds the time.
Butsudan. A household altar cabinet: the home shrine, small, clean and high, with an image, a candle, incense, a flower and water.
Your line: a quiet corner. Today, clear one small space, even a few inches of shelf, and keep it clean. Put one thing there that reminds you to practice. Day one hundred thirty-nine.

140.title: Three bows
140.hook: one for the Buddha, one for the dhamma, one for the sangha; bowing as setting pride down
140.howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists commonly bow three times with the five-point bow before a shrine or a monk; Zen practitioners bow with palms together, and Tibetan Buddhists may make full-length prostrations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, butsudan, the home shrine: an image, a candle, incense, a flower, water, somewhere high and clean. Your line was a quiet corner. Did you clear a few inches of shelf? Day one hundred forty.

For some first-time visitors, bowing is the hardest part of a temple. Sitting in silence, fine. Chanting, sure. But a forehead on the cool temple floor? Something in the chest can go stiff. I don't bow to anyone. And that stiffness, Buddhist teachers would say, is exactly the point. The bow isn't about who's above you. It's about what you're carrying. Today: three bows, and what gets set down with them.
screen: `SILENCE, FINE. CHANTING, SURE.` → `FOREHEAD ON THE FLOOR?` → `WHAT ARE YOU CARRYING?`

segments.voice: In Theravada practice, people bow three times in front of the shrine, usually after the homage you learned two days ago. One bow for the Buddha, one for the dhamma, one for the sangha: the three refuges, in the body. The traditional bow is called the five-point bow. You kneel, sit back on your heels, bring your palms together at the chest, then lower yourself so that five points touch the floor: the forehead, the two forearms or hands, and the two knees. Then you come back up. Three times. The Pali word for this kind of respect is vandana. Other traditions bow differently. In Zen, people bow with palms together, a gesture called gassho in Japanese. In Tibetan Buddhism, practitioners may make full-length prostrations, stretching out flat on the floor, and some take them up as a whole practice of their own, counted out over months. Different forms, the same gesture: lowering the head. Why does that matter? Because the tradition names pride, mana in Pali, conceit, the sense of I am, as one of the last things to fall away on the whole path. The bow puts it down for a moment, on purpose, with the body. Your forehead, where the thinking seems to live, goes lower than your heart. Nobody is being worshiped as a god here. Buddhists say they're bowing to awakening, to the teaching, to the people who practice it, and to the possibility of those in themselves. Some teachers put it this way: an honest bow leaves a person lighter, not smaller, standing up with something heavy left on the floor.

segments.voice: If your body allows, kneel, or stay seated if that's better. Bring your palms together at the chest. Lower your head, as far as is comfortable, once for the Buddha, once for the dhamma, once for the sangha. Or if you'd rather, one for awakening, one for the truth, one for everyone walking toward it. Go slowly. Feel the head come lower than the heart. Then sit, and notice whatever is lighter. The bell holds the time.
Three bows. One for the Buddha, one for the dhamma, one for the sangha: the head lowered, pride set down for a moment.
Your line: bow. Today, bow three times, at a shrine, beside your bed, or just with a nod of the head, and notice what the stiffness in you says about it. Day one hundred forty.

fork.setup: you're kneeling at a shrine for the first time. how many points of the body touch the floor in the traditional Theravada bow?
fork.reveal: it's the five-point bow: forehead, both forearms or hands, and both knees, three times over.

original.note: Pali: homage, respectful salutation, including the bow; also the name of the chanting that goes with it.

trapdoor: what you thought: bowing means submitting to someone above you.
what it means: setting pride down with the body, one bow for each of the three jewels.
what a scholar hears: mana (conceit) is one of the fetters said to be abandoned only at full awakening, so the humble bow points at the very end of the path.

sources.ref: Mana as one of the ten fetters (e.g. Samyutta Nikaya 45.180)
